articles.title: Mortos em enchentes no Nepal e Tibete sobem para 273 | G1
articles.standfirst: Desastre atingiu vilarejos, estradas e prédios após uma avalanche de gelo e rochas provocar uma enxurrada; mais de 700 estrangeiros estão entre os desaparecidos.
articles.summary: Mais de 1.300 pessoas estão desaparecidas após avalanche de gelo e rochas provocar enxurrada na fronteira entre Nepal e China
articles.body:
O número de mortos nas enchentes e deslizamentos na fronteira entre o Nepal e o Tibete, na China , subiu para 273 nesta quinta-feira (27). Mais de 1.300 pessoas estão desaparecidas, segundo autoridades dos dois países. As equipes de resgate continuam as buscas em áreas cobertas por lama e escombros.

Do total de mortos, 270 foram registrados no Nepal e três no Tibete. O desastre aconteceu na quarta-feira (26) , depois que uma avalanche de gelo e rochas atingiu um rio e provocou uma enorme enxurrada de água, lama e destroços.

No Nepal, 823 pessoas continuam desaparecidas, segundo as autoridades. Entre elas estão 517 estrangeiros. Na região do Tibete, outras 558 pessoas estão desaparecidas, incluindo 260 estrangeiros, de acordo com a imprensa estatal chinesa.

Entre os estrangeiros desaparecidos no Nepal estão 178 indianos, 65 americanos, 53 ucranianos, 51 malaios, 35 australianos, 33 britânicos e 25 canadenses.

No Nepal, a enchente atingiu áreas próximas aos rios Trishuli e Bhote Koshi. A região de Gyirong, no Tibete, também foi atingida. Casas, estradas, pontes e instalações de energia foram danificadas ou destruídas.

Segundo o Serviço Geológico dos Estados Unidos (USGS), o desastre foi provocado pelo colapso de uma geleira , e não por um terremoto. A queda de gelo e rochas atingiu o rio e desencadeou o fluxo de água e detritos.

As equipes de resgate avançam com dificuldade pelas áreas atingidas. A lama e os escombros dificultam o acesso a vilarejos e comunidades isoladas.

O Exército nepalês realizou sobrevoos na região e resgatou dezenas de pessoas. Moradores de áreas próximas aos rios também receberam ordens para deixar suas casas.

Especialistas alertam ainda para o risco de uma nova inundação. Um bloqueio de detritos permanece em uma área mais alta do rio na fronteira entre Nepal e China.

"Como ainda há um bloqueio na parte alta do rio fronteiriço entre o Nepal e a China, as autoridades alertam que pode acontecer uma segunda inundação", afirmou à AFP Qianggong Zhang, diretor de riscos climáticos e ambientais do Centro Internacional para o Desenvolvimento Integrado das Montanhas (ICIMOD).

A presença de centenas de estrangeiros entre os desaparecidos aumentou a preocupação das autoridades. Muitos estavam na região como turistas ou em peregrinações.

O Departamento de Turismo do Nepal informou que 517 estrangeiros estão entre as pessoas desaparecidas no país. A Índia é o país com o maior número de cidadãos desaparecidos.

Os Estados Unidos anunciaram uma ajuda de US$ 500 mil, cerca de R$ 2,5 milhões, para as operações de emergência.

O presidente chinês, Xi Jinping , afirmou que a prioridade é encontrar e resgatar as pessoas desaparecidas.

As chuvas de monção, entre junho e setembro, provocam inundações e deslizamentos em várias partes do sul da Ásia. Cientistas afirmam que o aquecimento global pode aumentar a frequência e a intensidade de eventos extremos na região.

Imagens de drone mostram propriedades cobertas de lama após uma enchente repentina em Trishuli, distrito de Nuwakot, Nepal, em 27 de agosto de 2026 — Foto: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

articles.title: Desembargador que perdeu aposentadoria foi condenado a pagar R$ 9 milhões por enriquecimento ilícito | G1
articles.standfirst: Processo aponta que Arthur Del Guercio Filho recebeu R$ 4,5 milhões em créditos extras entre 2008 e 2013; R$ 2,48 milhões vieram de 352 depósitos em dinheiro sem identificação do depositante.
articles.summary: Processo aponta que Arthur Del Guercio Filho recebeu R$ 4,5 milhões em créditos extras entre 2008 e 2013; R$ 2,48 milhões vieram de 352 depósitos em dinheiro sem identificação do depositante.
articles.body:
Fachada do Tribunal de Justiça de São Paulo (TJ-SP), no Centro da capital paulista. — Foto: Divulgação

O desembargador aposentado Arthur Del Guercio Filho , que teve a aposentadoria cassada pelo Tribunal de Justiça de São Paulo (TJ-SP) , foi condenado também a pagar cerca de R$ 9 milhões por improbidade administrativa. O valor inclui R$ 4,5 milhões que a Justiça considerou terem sido acrescidos ilicitamente ao patrimônio dele e outros R$ 4,5 milhões de multa civil.

A condenação foi imposta em uma ação movida pelo Ministério Público de São Paulo e mantida pelo TJ-SP. O processo mostra que, entre janeiro de 2008 e abril de 2013, Del Guercio recebeu cerca de R$ 2,1 milhões em salários, enquanto outros créditos que entraram em suas contas somaram aproximadamente R$ 4,5 milhões .

Desse total, R$ 2,48 milhões tiveram origem em 352 depósitos em dinheiro sem identificação do depositante , segundo perícia realizada durante a investigação. O TJ-SP concluiu que os recursos eram incompatíveis com os rendimentos do desembargador e que não houve comprovação de origem lícita.

O g1 tentou contato com a defesa de Arthur Del Guercio Filho, mas não obteve retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem. Nos autos do processo, o desembargador sempre negou as irregularidades apontadas pelo Ministério Público e contestou as acusações de enriquecimento ilícito e recebimento de vantagens indevidas.

Além da devolução de R$ 4,5 milhões e da multa de igual valor, Del Guercio foi condenado à suspensão dos direitos políticos por dez anos e à proibição de contratar com o poder público ou receber benefícios e incentivos fiscais pelo mesmo período. A pena de perda da função pública foi convertida em cassação da aposentadoria .

Na última semana, o presidente do TJ-SP, desembargador Francisco Eduardo Loureiro, determinou o cumprimento da cassação, com efeitos a partir de 11 de agosto de 2026.

Del Guercio foi afastado do cargo em abril de 2013 , durante a apuração das acusações, e, em agosto de 2014, recebeu aposentadoria compulsória como punição em processo administrativo disciplinar. Em setembro de 2023, foi condenado em primeira instância por improbidade administrativa, quando a Justiça determinou, entre outras sanções, a cassação da aposentadoria. A condenação foi mantida pelo TJ-SP e, após o encerramento dos recursos, a cassação foi efetivada pelo tribunal em agosto de 2026, com efeitos a partir do dia 11. Assim, Del Guercio recebeu aposentadoria compulsória por quase 12 anos .

Na ação, o Ministério Público relatou que servidores do gabinete de Del Guercio eram usados para realizar depósitos em suas contas bancárias.

Segundo a acusação, os depósitos eram feitos semanalmente, em valores que variavam normalmente de R$ 5 mil a R$ 20 mil . Em algumas ocasiões, os pacotes continham R$ 40 mil ou R$ 55 mil em espécie .

O MP afirmou ainda que, quando a quantia ultrapassava R$ 9.999, os funcionários eram orientados a fracionar os depósitos.

A perícia financeira citada na decisão identificou 579 transações que somaram os R$ 4,5 milhões em créditos extras.

No julgamento da apelação, o TJ-SP afirmou que a movimentação bancária correspondia a mais de duas vezes os créditos salariais do desembargador e destacou a ausência de comprovação da origem lícita dos recursos.

O processo também reúne relatos de advogados que afirmaram ter recebido pedidos de dinheiro de Del Guercio enquanto tinham processos em julgamento no tribunal.

Em um dos episódios reconhecidos pela Justiça, o advogado José Carlos Fagoni foi ao gabinete do desembargador para entregar memoriais de um processo. Segundo os autos, Del Guercio afirmou que enfrentava problemas financeiros e pediu R$ 25 mil.

O escritório acabou entregando R$ 15 mil , valor que, segundo o processo, nunca foi devolvido.

Em outro caso, o advogado Roberto Weidenmüller Guerra recebeu um e-mail de Del Guercio pedindo R$ 30 mil. Depois de o advogado afirmar que não tinha o dinheiro, o desembargador teria reduzido o pedido para R$ 15 mil.

O valor foi transferido e também não teria sido devolvido.

Ao manter a condenação, o TJ-SP afirmou que houve solicitações de dinheiro feitas dentro das dependências do Poder Judiciário a advogados que procuravam o desembargador para tratar de processos, sem relação de proximidade entre eles.

O acórdão também destacou que os valores não foram devolvidos e que os advogados demonstraram receio de que uma negativa pudesse trazer consequências para seus clientes.

Del Guercio já havia sido acusado de pedir R$ 120 mil a uma mulher que tinha um processo sob julgamento.

O advogado Clito Fornaciari Jr. afirmou que o desembargador mostrou à cliente um voto favorável, mas disse que outros magistrados exigiam dinheiro para acompanhá-lo. A cliente recusou o pagamento e acabou derrotada por três votos a zero, incluindo voto contrário de Del Guercio.

O caso foi um dos episódios que levaram ao afastamento do desembargador em 2013.

A defesa de Del Guercio sustentou ao longo do processo que ele enfrentava graves dificuldades financeiras e endividamento e negou que os valores recebidos fossem decorrentes do exercício da função de magistrado.

Ao analisar o recurso, porém, o TJ-SP manteve a condenação por enriquecimento ilícito e por obtenção de vantagens indevidas relacionadas ao cargo.

articles.title: Terapia me ajudou a lembrar dos abusos que sofri do meu meio-irmão | G1
articles.standfirst: Mellissa Arkwright não conseguia se lembrar dos abusos sofridos quando era criança, até que um tipo específico de terapia liberou suas recordações.
articles.summary: Mellissa Arkwright não conseguia se lembrar dos abusos sofridos quando era criança, até que um tipo específico de terapia liberou suas recordações.
articles.body:
Nikita Dallison e Mellissa Arkwright abriram mão do anonimato para contar o que aconteceu com elas — Foto: Arquivo de família

Importante: esta reportagem contém detalhes de abuso infantil que podem ser perturbadores para alguns leitores.

As irmãs Nikita Dallison e Mellissa Arkwright tinham apenas seis e sete anos de idade quando começaram a sofrer abusos por parte do seu meio-irmão, Adrian Austin.

Dallison, hoje com 36 anos, se recorda claramente dos dolorosos detalhes. Mas Arkwright, com 35, ainda não conseguia se lembrar do que tinha acontecido com ela quando era criança.

Foi somente quando Dallison denunciou corajosamente os abusos à polícia em 2021, que Arkwright decidiu se submeter a uma terapia conhecida como dessensibilização e reprocessamento por meio dos movimentos oculares (EMDR, na sigla em inglês).

O procedimento consiste em ouvir sons, dar pequenos golpes ou acender e apagar luzes de forma intermitente, para fazer a pessoa se lembrar de um evento traumático.

"Eu precisava da terapia porque minha saúde mental havia se desmoronado por completo... mas nunca entendi por quê", conta Arkwright.

"Submeter-se a ela [terapia] é horrível, porque você sente absolutamente tudo."

"Quando você recebe a terapia, pode sentir o ambiente que havia no quarto" no momento em que a lembrança foi desbloqueada, explica ela.

A terapia EMDR ajudou Arkwright a recuperar uma recordação específica, que acabou sendo fundamental para as provas que levaram à condenação de seu meio-irmão.

Austin tem hoje 45 anos. Ele foi preso em julho e condenado a 17 anos de prisão após ser declarado culpado de seis acusações de manter relações sexuais com uma menina menor de 13 anos, o que é classificado como estupro segundo as leis sobre crimes sexuais vigentes no Reino Unido.

Ele também foi declarado culpado de quatro crimes de agressão sexual e de um crime de atos indecentes com uma pessoa menor de idade, cometidos entre 1997 e 2001.

"Relembrar o dia em que ele foi condenado ainda me perturba, pois conseguimos justiça para aquelas meninas", declarou Arkwright.

"Foi algo surreal e acredito que nunca chorei tanto quanto naquele dia. Foi como se tivessem tirado um grande peso de cima dos meus ombros. Eu sabia que tudo havia terminado. Ele não pode prejudicar mais ninguém", afirma ela.

Mellissa Arkwright e Nikita Dallison, em 1996 — Foto: Arquivo de família

As vítimas de crimes sexuais têm automaticamente direito ao anonimato no Reino Unido. Mas as irmãs abriram mão deste direito para poderem contar a sua história.

Os abusos começaram quando Austin se mudou para a casa da família em Manchester, na Inglaterra, aos 10 anos de idade. Antes, ele morava com o pai.

"Ele se comportava de forma inadequada", conta Dallison. "Ele nos pedia para mostrar nossa roupa de baixo, esse tipo de coisas, e a situação foi piorando até que ele chegou a nos tocar."

Ela relembra o "medo, confusão e pavor" que sentiu quando era criança. E, em pouco tempo, ele começou a abusar das irmãs, segundo ela.

Após anos de silêncio, Dallison decidiu denunciar à polícia o que aconteceu.

Na época, seus filhos tinham a mesma idade que ela quando sofreu os abusos. Dallison não conseguia compreender como alguém poderia ser tão cruel.

Ela também acreditava que a saúde mental de Arkwright havia se deteriorado drasticamente ao reviver as recordações do abuso, sem ter consciência de que não conseguia se lembrar do que havia acontecido.

O inspetor Chris Preston, da polícia da região metropolitana de Manchester, contou que primeiro ouviu Dallison e depois conversou com cautela com Arkwright, que passava por uma crise de saúde mental e não se lembrava dos abusos.

Mas, à medida que a investigação avançava, Arkwright contou a única recordação que havia recuperado, graças à terapia EMDR.

"Este tipo de terapia é novo para nós e precisamos investigar um pouco para descobrir o significado exato dela", explica Preston.

A terapia EMDR foi realizada por uma pessoa que passou a atuar como perito no julgamento.

"Seu testemunho foi muito claro. Foi um testemunho incrível, que explicou a terapia EMDR com muita clareza", relatou, lembrando que Melissa conseguiu recuperar uma recordação muito específica.

"Ela pôde descrever o quarto, o estrado da cama, o espaço entre os dentes de Adrian Austin quando ele cometia seus crimes horríveis. Esta confirmação é muito importante", segundo Preston.

O Tribunal Real de Manchester condenou Adrian Austin a 17 anos de prisão — Foto: GMP

Durante a investigação, soube-se também que a polícia havia ouvido Mellissa Arkwright sobre os abusos em 1997, mas o caso não foi adiante.

As circunstâncias exatas não são conhecidas. A polícia acredita que seus pais tenham denunciado o abuso aos policiais, mas se colocado ao lado de Austin.

Em 2021, a investigação da polícia da região metropolitana de Manchester revelou que os pais das irmãs tinham conhecimento do abuso.

"O nosso lema familiar era 'o que acontece na família fica na família', mas não é mais", conta Arkwright.

"Eles sempre diziam isso. Mas, agora, não fico mais calada. Sempre me chamavam de mentirosa, de dramática. Agora, não importa mais. Vou dizer o que tiver que dizer."

A conversa da polícia com Melissa em 1997 foi gravada em vídeo e encontrada em uma fita VHS em um armazém policial repleto de caixas, do piso até o teto. Ela também foi incluída entre as provas do julgamento.

Austin se mudou de casa depois disso, mas continuou tomando conta das irmãs no seu apartamento em Manchester.

A polícia o interrogou diversas vezes. Ele continuava negando o crime e alegava que as irmãs nunca estiveram no seu apartamento.

Mas Nikita Dallison conseguiu descrever a distribuição exata dos cômodos, que coincidia com os registros do local.

Dallison sentiu enorme alívio quando o júri anunciou o veredito considerando Austin culpado. E também por saber que sua irmã não se lembrava de tudo o que havia acontecido com elas.

"Não falamos disso nem mesmo hoje, porque tenho total consciência de que Mellissa não tem essas lembranças", conta Dallison. "Isso me conforta muito, na verdade."

"Achei muito estranho quando fiquei sabendo. Pensei que ela simplesmente estivesse escondendo e que não quisesse falar", afirma.

"Mas sei que, agora, ela sabe de algumas coisas, depois do que aconteceu no julgamento. É triste, mas me consola muito o fato de que ela não tenha tudo na memória."

Mellissa Arkwright e Nikita Dallison, fotografadas em 1994, antes de Austin se mudar para a casa delas — Foto: Arquivo de família

A detetive Rebecca Lovekin declarou que as irmãs demonstraram "enorme ccoragem, apoio e disposição durante este processo".

"O simples fato de denunciar esses crimes foi um passo enorme para elas", destacou Lovekin.

"Compreendemos que foi difícil para as duas quando a investigação inicial de 1997, não seguiu até o ponto a que deveria ter chegado. Reconhecemos este fato e pedimos desculpas a elas pela forma como aquela investigação foi conduzida na época", destacou.

"Desde então, nós progredimos e a forma de investigação de abusos sexuais, particularmente do abuso sexual histórico, evoluiu consideravelmente, com maior compreensão das experiências dos sobreviventes."

"A polícia da região metropolitana de Manchester, hoje, fez justiça para as meninas e colocou Austin atrás das grades", conclui Rebecca Lovekin.

articles.title: Em 2015, Nepal sofreu com ‘o pior terremoto em mais de 80 anos’ até então; número de mortos passou de 8,5 mil | G1
articles.standfirst: A equipe do programa ‘Planeta Extremo’ estava no país e foi surpreendida pelo tremor no meio de uma estrada: ‘Gritos, desespero’. Veja no Arquivo JN.
articles.summary: A equipe do programa ‘Planeta Extremo’ estava no país e foi surpreendida pelo tremor no meio de uma estrada: ‘Gritos, desespero’. Veja no Arquivo JN.
articles.body:
China e Nepal enfrentaram a fúria da natureza. Nesta quarta-feira (26), o Jornal Nacional mostrou que uma avalanche de gelo, pedra e lama provocou uma enxurrada que varreu vilarejos na fronteira entre os dois países. Os vales em “V” fizeram com que avalanche ganhasse ainda mais força , como em um funil.

As causas desse desastre ainda estão sendo investigadas. O Centro Geológico dos EUA explicou que, na verdade, não teve terremoto. É que o deslizamento foi tão forte que os sensores registraram o impacto como se tivesse havido um tremor.

Este texto e o vídeo acima são parte da série Arquivo JN no g1, que relembra coberturas importantes relacionadas a temas atuais.

Terremoto atinge o Nepal em abril de 2015 — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Em abril de 2015, o Nepal enfrentou uma outra tragédia: um terremoto arrasou quase metade do país montanhoso no sul da Ásia. Na época, o tremor foi classificado como “o pior terremoto no Nepal em mais de 80 anos”. O número de mortos passou de 8,5 mil .

A equipe do programa “Planeta Extremo”, da TV Globo, estava no Nepal e foi surpreendida pelo terremoto no meio de uma estrada.

“Tivemos que abandonar o ônibus e correr o mais rápido que podíamos para fugir da área de risco. Gritos, desespero. Moradores fugindo de casa, correndo pela estrada sem saber para onde. Vimos casas despedaçadas”, relatou o repórter Clayton Conservani.

articles.title: Lito Sousa começou carreira na aviação aos 14 anos no litoral de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Piloto e mecânico de aeronaves luta por tratamento experimental após ser diagnosticado com a doença Creutzfeld-Jacob. Ele começou a estudar aviação e fez estágio em Guarujá (SP).
articles.summary: Piloto e mecânico de aeronaves luta por tratamento experimental após ser diagnosticado com a doença Creutzfeld-Jacob. Ele começou a estudar aviação e fez estágio em Guarujá (SP).
articles.body:
Lito Sousa , piloto e mecânico de aeronaves diagnosticado com a doença Creutzfeldt-Jakob (DCJ) , começou a carreira na Base Aérea de Santos , no litoral de São Paulo . Ele ficou conhecido na internet ao produzir vídeos sobre aviação no canal do Youtube Aviões e Músicas, no qual acumula mais de 3 milhões de seguidores.

🔎A DCJ é uma doença priônica humana — rara, neurodegenerativa, progressiva e sem cura. O quadro costuma começar com demência, perda de memória e tremores, e evolui com outros sinais neurológicos que afetam diferentes regiões do cérebro simultaneamente. Existem quatro formas conhecidas de DCJ: esporádica, hereditária, iatrogênica e a nova variante (vDCJ).

O diagnóstico do influenciador foi divulgado pela esposa dele na última semana e, desde então, a busca da família por um tratamento experimental repercutiu em todo o mundo. Nesta terça-feira (25), o ministro da Saúde, Alexandre Padilha, afirmou que a pasta formalizou um pedido para incluir Lito na fase inicial de um estudo nos Estados Unidos.

Lito Sousa compartilhou sobre início da carreira na aviação nas redes sociais — Foto: Reprodução/Redes sociais

A Baixada Santista fez parte do início da trajetória de Lito no universo do aeromotor. Em uma publicação nas redes sociais, o influenciador afirmou que fez a primeira aula no curso técnico de Manutenção de Aeronaves em 1982, na Base Aérea de Santos, localizada em Guarujá .

Na época, Lito era adolescente. "Mal sabia que esse dia seria o primeiro dia de uma carreira de quase 40 anos na aviação”, escreveu o influenciador, na publicação divulgada em novembro de 2024.

Lito Sousa gravou vídeo na Base Aérea de Santos em 2019 — Foto: Reprodução/Youtube

Antes disso, o mecânico de aeronaves havia compartilhado registros de uma visita à Base Aérea de Santos realizada em 2019, durante um evento de aviação. Na ocasião, ele reforçou que se formou como mecânico de aeronaves no local.

No vídeo, ele mostrou o hangar onde fez estágio e relembrou memórias do início da carreira, mostrando diversos pontos da Base Aérea, como o local onde ele engraxava rolamentos de roda de avião.

O ex-piloto e influenciador Lito Sousa, em vídeo publicado em 23 de agosto de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução/ Instagram

Joselito Geraldo de Sousa, de 59 anos, trabalhou em funções ligadas à manutenção e à segurança de aviões em empresas como Varig, Transbrasil e United Airlines.

Após décadas trabalhando na manutenção, realizou o sonho de se tornar piloto e obteve sua habilitação em 2021.

Lito Sousa é o nome profissional do piloto Joselito Geraldo de Sousa, de 59 anos, um dos principais influenciadores brasileiros especializados em aviação. — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Lito também é escritor e atua como palestrante e consultor, usando conceitos da aviação para falar sobre segurança, fatores humanos e gestão de riscos.

Ao lado da esposa, a empresária Mila Seidl, ele criou a Lito Academy, empresa que administra cursos, palestras e consultorias.

Lito Sousa é dono do canal 'Aviões e Músicas', no YouTube, onde explica, em linguagem acessível, como funcionam aviões, procedimentos de segurança, turbulências e acidentes aéreos. — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

articles.title: Bill Gates is sounding the alarm about growing risks posed by AI
articles.summary: “This is like an evolutionary milestone that needs incredible policy management by society as a whole,” he said.
articles.body: SAN FRANCISCO — Bill Gates is looking to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping later this year, eager to propose global efforts to mitigate the growing risks posed by artificial intelligence. The Microsoft co-founder and billionaire philanthropist told Reuters in an interview that he believes China might agree to restricting potentially dangerous AI model releases if the U.S. took the initiative. “The whole world would go along with that,” said Gates, who met with Xi three years ago, when he was the first foreign entrepreneur to be hosted by the Chinese president post-pandemic. Gates also said he’d like to propose that countries monitor AI’s ability to create molecules and carry out biological attacks — something that would not get in the way of any tech industry’s development. Gates’ staff is working to finalize a meeting with Xi for his next China trip, his spokesperson said, scheduled tentatively for November. Xi “might be surprised by how vehement I am,” Gates said. He said China is protecting children from AI companion addiction, but he believes few leaders globally are rising to the occasion to get ahead of a litany of potential harms from AI. “Yes, in the past, technology never did this. This time is different. This is like an evolutionary milestone that needs incredible policy management by society as a whole.” China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. AI hacking ‘should blow people’s minds’ Gates struck a more optimistic note about AI in January, but since then he has become concerned that it can conduct attacks while supplanting jobs and hooking users psychologically. For instance, technology from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms META.O recently hacked real-world websites in what were supposed to be isolated cybersecurity evaluations. “These security incidents are shocking, and they should blow people’s minds,” Gates said. In a blog post on Wednesday, Gates called for a new international organization to manage AI, drawing on elements from a nuclear inspections regime, international aviation regulations and ozone layer protection agreements. To date, President Donald Trump’s administration has exercised some control over the distribution of powerful AI models such as Anthropic’s Fable 5, but more regulation has taken place at the state level. Whereas many tech leaders have, like Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, touted the benefits of AI, many have also expressed concern about its perils. Demis Hassabis, chair of Google DeepMind GOOGL.O, proposed a body like the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, or FINRA, that could develop and conduct tests of AI related to national security. Gates agrees with others that the United States should take the lead but says it must establish what criteria would determine what action. “You can use a FINRA-type model, but it’s a silly conversation,” Gates said. “It’s like saying, ‘Should we meet to discuss taxation at this restaurant or this restaurant?’” ‘World’s top priority’ In his blog post, Gates said it was the “world’s top priority” to deliver an AI future that does not widen inequality and hurt the vulnerable, ahead of climate change and health crises. As he pursues high-profile engagements, Gates also told Reuters he planned to see U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham this autumn. In February, he canceled an appearance in India after the U.S. released files from sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Gates has said he did not realize ​the extent of Epstein’s crimes when associating with him for philanthropy. His foundation is aiming to spend $200 billion by 2045 with an increasing focus on AI. It is working with Anthropic on AI-powered health checks for pregnancy and with OpenAI to help healthcare workers in Rwanda, Gates said. He also will speak to personnel at Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which are preparing blockbuster IPOs, about impactful giving, he said. On his mind are various ideas for addressing social upheaval. He envisioned taxing revenue from companies using “tokens” or AI’s outputs to supplant labor, which could help fund a safety net. He also said society should reserve up to 40% of current jobs for humans, noting in the blog how care his dad received when suffering from Alzheimer’s disease was “irreplaceably human.” Gates said community protests centered on data centers were missing a bigger picture. “Wait until you really screw up the job market,” he said.

images.caption: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates arrives for a closed-door interview with the House Oversight Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, on June 10, 2026.

articles.title: Tim Curry, star of The Rocky Horror Picture Show, dies at age 80
articles.summary: Curry, a three-time Tony nominee, was best known for his portrayal of Dr Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic musical.
articles.body:
Tim Curry, the British actor best known for his star turn as Dr Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic musical The Rocky Horror Picture Show, has died at age 80.

Curry, who had struggled with his health for more than a decade after a debilitating stroke, died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, California, according to a statement released by his longtime manager, Marcia Hurwitz, on Wednesday. No cause of death was disclosed.

The actor appeared in numerous movies, often as a hammy villain. He was nominated at the annual Tony Awards three times for Broadway roles and performed voice work in several animated films and television shows.

But his most iconic role was as Frank-N-Furter, a cross-dressing scientist in the rock musical The Rocky Horror Show, which premiered in 1973 at the Royal Court Theatre in London.

He took the show-stopping role to Broadway and then reprised his turn as Frank-N-Furter in the 1975 film adaptation, alongside Barry Bostwick, Meat Loaf and Susan Sarandon.

“I’m not much of a man by the light of day. But by night, I’m one hell of a lover. I’m just a sweet transvestite from transsexual Transylvania,” Curry sang in one scene, dressed in garish eye shadow, black corsetry and stockings topped with a garter belt.

In a 1975 television interview, Curry noted the risk of having his career defined by the role.

“When I read it, I just thought it was very, very witty and funny,” Curry said of the script, although he confessed to some initial reluctance to star in the role.

“I mean, I was hesitant in that, if it worked, it might be a difficult thing to shake off. But, really, I’ve always thought that [a part] wasn’t worth doing unless you took a risk.”

He later starred as the child-killing monster in the 1990 miniseries It, an adaptation of Stephen King’s horror novel.

That same year, he performed as a Soviet medical officer in the film The Hunt for Red October, based on the Cold War-era novel by Tom Clancy.

Later, he lent sneering gravitas to the role of the double-dealing Cardinal Richelieu in the 1993 adventure movie The Three Musketeers, with Kiefer Sutherland, Charlie Sheen and Chris O’Donnell.

“Tim Curry was someone I cared deeply about, he was someone I loved working with and I am so lucky to have these memories,” Sutherland said in a statement on Wednesday.

Born in the English village of Grappenhall, Cheshire, Curry studied drama at Birmingham University.

Critics argue he did much of his best work on stage. His first Tony nomination came in 1981 for his performance in the title role of Amadeus, a play fictionalising the great composer Mozart’s interactions with his rival, Antonio Salieri.

A second Tony nod came in 1993 for his leading role in the musical My Favorite Year. In 2005, he scooped up a third nomination for his portrayal of King Arthur in the zany musical Monty Python’s Spamalot.

Having a rich baritone voice, he was also in demand as a voice actor for animated films and television shows. He won a Daytime Emmy Award in 1991 for his voice work on the animated series Peter Pan and the Pirates.

Curry withdrew from a British stage production in 2011 due to ill health. In 2013, his agent said that he had suffered a stroke but was recovering “in great humor”.

From then on, he used a wheelchair and reduced his workload. In 2024, however, he returned to the big screen, appearing in the horror film Stream.

Curry, who lived in Los Angeles, never married and had no children. A composer and a singer, Curry also performed with his own rock band and released a handful of albums.

articles.title: HEAR IT: 911 call captures horrifying first moments of deadly shooting at Seattle’s Bite of Seattle festival
articles.summary: Newly obtained 911 calls reveal the chaos at the Bite of Seattle shooting, with dispatchers reporting six confirmed gunshot wounds near the Space Needle.
articles.body: Newly obtained 911 calls shed new light on the deadly shooting at Seattle’s famed Bite of Seattle festival, capturing the frantic response as first responders raced to help with multiple people down. "I’m losing blood," a caller who described being shot in the back told a dispatcher. The caller did not know who had opened fire. GUNFIRE SHATTERS TORONTO LATIN STREET FESTIVAL LEAVING AT LEAST 2 DEAD AND MULTIPLE WOUNDED "I don’t know who did it. I took cover. I see the officers down here," the caller said. The dispatcher tried to keep the wounded person calm as help was sent toward the water fountain where the caller was believed to be waiting. "It’s OK. Just breathe. Breathe with me. I’m going to stay with you," the dispatcher said. Moments later, the caller spoke of being with an officer. Other emergency transmissions capture dispatchers and first responders working to assess the scope of the unfolding violence near the Seattle Center Armory. "Multiple people down at this point," one dispatcher said when asked whether anyone had been shot. TOLEDO POLICE FOLLOWING 'MULTIPLE LEADS' AS MANHUNT ENTERS 3RD DAY AFTER FESTIVAL SHOOTING As reports continued to come in, another dispatcher requested "as many aid units as possible," saying there were at least two people down "but more than that." Emergency crews initially treated the area as an active scene while officials worked to determine whether it was safe for responders to enter. "Let’s treat that as an active scene for now," a dispatcher said. A dispatcher later said there were "six confirmed gunshot wounds" amid the chaotic response. MULTIPLE PEOPLE KILLED IN SHOOTING AT IDAHO IN-N-OUT RESTAURANT, SUSPECT DEAD The calls come as Seattle police have offered few public updates on the investigation. Fox 13 Seattle reported that interim Police Chief Andre Sayles said earlier this month that investigators had developed new information and expected to make an arrest, but he declined to disclose details. SEATTLE MAYOR'S INTERVIEW CUT SHORT AS STAFF BLOCKS QUESTIONS ON GUN VIOLENCE, SURVEILLANCE "I think the biggest thing is, you know, it’s going to cause a little bit of frustration, is the integrity of this investigation," Sayles said Aug. 7, according to the outlet. "There’s some information that we have. I want to make sure that we keep the integrity of that investigation close to the vest until we can make the appropriate arrest." A 15-year-old suspect remains in custody in the shooting. TWO TEEN SUSPECTS HELD AFTER 5 FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN 'TARGETED MASS SHOOTING' The Mayor’s Office said in a statement to the outlet that the administration "continues to work closely with the Seattle Police Department to ensure information about critical events reach(es) the public." The shooting erupted last month outside the Seattle Center Armory during the Bite of Seattle food festival near the Space Needle. Three people were killed, and four others were wounded, including a 2-year-old boy, authorities previously said. The dead included a 19-year-old man and a 44-year-old man who were pronounced dead at the scene. A 56-year-old woman later died after she was transported to a hospital in critical condition. Wilson called the shooting "an act of horrific violence." "Impacted families are living through the worst moment of their lives, and an entire community is trying to understand how a gathering built around culture, connection and joy ended in gunfire," Wilson said at the time. "No one should have to weigh the risk of being shot before attending an event, gathering with friends, or experiencing their city." Wilson said officials believed a 15-year-old had opened fire into the crowd, though details remained under investigation. The teen was booked into juvenile detention on suspicion of gun violations and first-degree assault. No homicide charges had been filed as of the most recent update. Former Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes said investigators believed gunfire was exchanged outside the Armory after a conflict involving small groups believed to be at odds with one another, leaving bystanders caught in the crossfire. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Investigators initially believed two gunmen were involved. But a juvenile court document later indicated the detained teen and an acquaintance who was found dead at the scene may have exchanged gunfire with at least one other, unidentified suspect. Fox News Digital reached out to the Seattle Police Department and mayor's office for comment.

articles.title: 'View' host Ana Navarro rejects Hunter Biden's assertion that Trump is 'already' a 'dictator'
articles.summary: Ana Navarro pushed back after Hunter Biden declared on her podcast that democracy was "gone" under President Donald Trump in contrast to some of her past comments.
articles.body: "The View" co-host Ana Navarro appeared to disagree with former President Joe Biden's son, Hunter Biden, after he accused President Donald Trump of being a dictator on her podcast Monday. In the second half of a two-part interview on "Bleep! with Ana Navarro," Hunter Biden told Navarro the U.S. has "already" lost democracy under Trump regardless of who wins the midterm elections. "He is a dictator ... in no uncertain terms," Biden said. "Everybody understands this. He has broken the system. It is gone. It is completely broken." 'THE VIEW' CO-HOST LAUDS HUNTER BIDEN AS 'RIVETING' AFTER PODCAST SIT-DOWN, CALLS HIM 'BIGGEST TROLL' "They’re going through confirmation hearings right now of his personal attorney to be the attorney general of the United States," he continued. "He has used his position as president of the United States to jail, to attempt to jail journalists. He is prosecuting Don Lemon for following someone into … and we’re not all sitting here up in arms?" Trump's former personal attorney and acting Attorney General Todd Blanche was confirmed as attorney general earlier this month. Lemon has pleaded not guilty to federal civil rights charges stemming from his coverage of an anti-ICE protest that disrupted a church service in St. Paul, Minnesota. Lemon maintains he was there as a journalist. "He goes on Air Force One, and he gets a question that he doesn’t like, and he looks at a veteran woman reporter and tells her to ‘Be quiet, piggy,’ and no one says anything," Biden added. "We have lost our democracy at this point." "Can you imagine if your father had ever done that?" Navarro asked. "I can't even remotely imagine," Biden said. However, Navarro stopped short of calling Trump a dictator, though she said "he would like to be." "I fled dictatorship," she said. "I fled the Sandinistas in 1980, and I live in Miami, where there’s a lot of Cuban-American exiles, a lot of Venezuelan-American exiles, a lot of Haitian-American exiles. I think he definitely would like to be a dictator and have no guardrails, have no pushback. "I still have some hope in some of the courts. And I think we still have elections. And despite the fact that there's threats against the free press, we still do have the free press." ANA NAVARRO AND FORMER TRUMP CAMPAIGN AIDE CLASH OVER PRESIDENT'S COMBATIVE EXCHANGES WITH FEMALE JOURNALISTS She argued that the larger problem was a lack of congressional oversight from Republicans to balance out Trump's power and questioned whether Democrats retaking the House and Senate could make a difference. "I don't know that they have the stomach to do some of the s--- that Republicans do without any qualms," Navarro said. Navarro's response on the podcast marked a stark departure from her past comments on Trump, when she warned of him behaving like a dictator and suggested his actions were dictatorial. During her speech at the 2024 Democratic National Convention, Navarro compared Trump to several communist dictators. "Let me tell you what communist dictators do, and it's never just for one day," she said at the time. "They attack the free press. They call them the enemy of the people like Ortega does in Nicaragua. They put their unqualified relatives in cushy government jobs so they can get rich off their positions like the Castros do in Cuba. "And they refuse to accept legitimate elections when they lose and call for violence to stay in power like Maduro is doing right now in Venezuela," Navarro continued. "Now, you tell me something. Do any of those things sound familiar? Is there anybody running for president who reminds you of that?" DAN RATHER AMONG 200 JOURNALISTS DEMANDING TRUMP BE CALLED OUT AT WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER As recently as May, Navarro accused Trump on "The View" of being a "wannabe dictator" or having "small dictator energy" after a golden statue of Trump was installed at Trump National Doral golf course after the PGA Tour's Cadillac Championship. Fox News Digital reached out to Navarro for comment but did not immediately receive a response. White House spokesperson Davis Ingle dismissed the suggestion that Trump was a dictator and mocked Hunter Biden in a statement. articles.title: From Tokyo to London, heatwaves send men to work in shorts
articles.summary: Europe News: WARSAW/LONDON: Scorching summer temperatures have done what decades of dress-down Fridays have failed to do — get men to the office in shorts.Japan’s .
articles.body: WARSAW/LONDON: Scorching summer temperatures have done what decades of dress-down Fridays have failed to do — get men to the office in shorts.Japan’s capital led the way. This year the metropolitan govt’s long-standing no-tie, no-jacket “Cool Biz” campaign took a step further by encouraging its staff to ditch long trousers, and even try T-shirts and sneakers.As heatwaves mounted across Europe, other workers followed in Tokyo’s wake, sometimes with the encouragement of authorities and management, sometimes without.Major retailers said linen shorts and suits were flying off the shelves in Britain, as men opted for breathable fabrics more commonly associated with Mediterranean climes. “The lines between ‘commuter’ and ‘holiday’ style are blurring,” Martha Hibberd, menswear buyer at British department store John Lewis, said.Marks and Spencer said sales of men’s linen trousers in June to July jumped 183% compared with the same period a year ago. H&M — one of Europe’s biggest fashion retailers — said it was bringing in lighter clothes and delaying the release of autumnal lines to later in the year. “It looks like we’re not going back when it comes to climate change,” Andreas Lowenstam, H&M’s head of menswear design, said.Hugo Boss said it has increased its assortment of tailored shorts. Its “Boss by Beckham” range in collaboration with soccer star David Beckham offers a pair of cotton tailored shorts for ¤229.The trend was there to see in Europe’s business hubs, from London’s Canary Wharf to the streets of Frankfurt. But there were some limits. At Norway’s largest bank, DNB, staff were welcome to wear shorts and skirts, spokesperson Vidar Korsberg Dalsbo told Reuters. “However, we are probably talking about smarter garments with some length rather than a ballerina skirt or a cheeky pair of 1970s-style soccer shorts.”In June, Gianfranco Lot, Switzerland head at insurance group Swiss Re, wrote an email to staff with tips on how to stay cool. Alongside the list of suggestions — such as drinking water, breaking when needed, and taking a dip in Lake Zurich just across from the office — there was a quick reminder that “shorts are for weekends”.Pushing back against the traditions, there were signs that some workers were prepared to take a stand for their lighter attire.Germany’s biggest union, IG Metall, and services sector union Verdi both said they believed dress codes should be relaxed or waived if necessary at times of higher temperatures. “Summers are getting hotter, heat waves are becoming more frequent, and the strain on workers is noticeably increasing,” Moriz Tiedemann, occupational health expert at IG Metall, said.Some were already taking matters into their own hands. In Warsaw, one bus driver decided he had had enough of the standard uniform of long polyester trousers and turned up to work one day this month in a skirt as a protest. “These materials make us sweat and overheat,” said the man, who only gave his name as Darek.At the last count, a petition launched by one of his colleagues, asking the Polish capital’s transport authority ZTM to let drivers wear shorts during hot weather, had collected over 400 signatures.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: NYC business owners revolt over Mamdani’s government-run grocery stores: ‘Doomed for disaster'
articles.summary: Bodega owners rallied in Harlem to oppose Zohran Mamdani's city-run grocery stores, filing two lawsuits that allege civil rights violations.
articles.body: New York City business leaders and bodega owners rallied Wednesday just steps away from the future site of one of Mayor Zohran Mamdani's city-run grocery stores, arguing the plan will force local businesses to close. The Multicultural Business Coalition, which is made up of 50 chambers of commerce representing multicultural businesses, filed two lawsuits in state court on Monday challenging Mamdani’s plan to open five government-owned supermarkets with subsidized grocery offerings. On Wednesday, leaders within the coalition gathered alongside bodega owners outside the American Deli Mini Market Corp, in Harlem — which sits across the street from the confirmed Manhattan city-run store location at La Marqueta — to challenge Mamdani’s rollout of the stores, which is slated to begin in late-2027. GROCERY BOSS WARNS MAMDANI'S CITY-RUN STORES PIT GOVERNMENT AGAINST 'ITS OWN CITIZENS' "This is a campaign promise doomed for disaster if it is allowed to go through," Mark Jaffe, president and CEO of the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce, told Fox News Digital. One of the two lawsuits is a seven-page class-action filed on behalf of "hundreds" of store owners and alleges the opening of the city-run grocery stores would violate the businesses’ civil rights, according to court documents. "When you use government money discriminatorily, it could be a civil rights violation," Jaffe said, adding, "Shame on the [Mamdani] administration for not working with small businesses, but trying to hurt them and being heartless in their statements." The second suit asks the courts to permanently block the operation of "the municipal grocery stores, in absence of undertaking necessary studies and analysis," a move that has historically barred large retailers — such as Walmart — from entering the Big Apple. 'WASTEFUL DISTRACTION': EXPERTS SLAM MAMDANI'S TAXPAYER-FUNDED GROCERY STORES Under Mamdani’s plan, the five grocery stores will offer a core basket of items priced 30% below the average retail prices sold at other businesses. "Under the model, the City will own the land and cover overhead costs like rent and construction. A private operator, selected through a request for proposals, will manage daily operations and be contractually required to pass savings directly to customers on a core basket of everyday staples," an April news release stated. However, the pricing and subsidization of business expenses for the city-run stores puts the operators at an unfair advantage, according to Jaffe. EXPERTS SCORCH MAMDANI'S GROCERY PLAN AS AN 'ILLUSION' THAT WILL HAVE TAXPAYERS FOOTING THE BILL "It’s unfair," Jaffe told Fox News Digital. "[Small business owners] who have to pay their Con Edison bill, their real estate taxes, their fines and full price for food cannot compete." "The end-game here would be to help [small businesses owners] and not just subsidize 30% off from suppliers who are not lowering their prices for the city," he continued. "Our tax dollars are buying groceries at full price, so we can sell them at 30% off up the street — that’s not going to feed enough struggling people." Jaffe added that he believes the solution could lie in the establishment of a task force focused on mitigating the damage to local businesses in the surrounding areas of each store. "The only reason [small businesses] are going to be hurt is because [Mamdani] is taking tax dollars to put [them] out of business," Jaffe told Fox News Digital. "It's wrong. We want a task force. We'll show you how to feed struggling people." GROCER-TURNED-LAWMAKER SAYS MAMDANI’S GOVERNMENT-RUN STORES 'MIGHT NOT EVEN LAST A YEAR’ As part of the rollout of the city's government-run grocery stores, Mamdani established the NYC Groceries Task Force to "convene city agencies, industry experts and local small business owners to guide implementation," the administration said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Additionally, the city launched an OPEN Task Force to "identify and eliminate unnecessary red tape and reduce fines and fees for small businesses," according to Mamdani's office. The sentiment surrounding the stores' impacts on local businesses was echoed by Elvis, the owner of American Deli Mini Market Corp, identified only by his first name. "If [Mamdani opens this store] in front of [my] business, [I’m] going to go out of business," Elvis said through a translator at the press conference. "[I] pay a lot of taxes and this is not fair." NYC GROCERS SOUND ALARM ON MAMDANI'S SUPERMARKET PLAN: 'WE'LL LOSE CUSTOMERS' MAMDANI'S GROCERY GIVEAWAY HITS ID SNAG AS CRITICS CRY FOUL: 'MAKE IT MAKE SENSE' Mamdani has long defended his plan for government-run grocery stores, saying Monday that he is "fully confident in both the legality and the importance of our initiative." "The administration plans to open one city grocery store in each borough by the end of the Mayor's first term. There are more than 1,000 grocery stores and supermarkets and over 10,000 bodegas and corner stores across New York City," Mamdani's office said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "There are more than 1.4 million New Yorkers currently struggling with food insecurity. The five city grocery stores will not have a significant impact on the hundreds of grocery stores or the thousands of bodegas across the city." However, Jaffe insists the opening of the city-run, subsidized stores will do more harm than good to the surrounding businesses and will ultimately drive the minority entrepreneurs out of the Big Apple. History shows us that communist supermarkets have empty shelves," Jaffe said, adding, "We have better ways to help feed the struggling people. Please listen, Mr. Mayor. Don't keep campaign promises that will hurt people."

articles.title: Brazil sues chat platform Discord over failure to protect child users
articles.summary: Lawsuit is latest instance of Brazil taking aggressive steps to rein in tech giants over child safety issues online.
articles.body:
The Brazilian government has filed a lawsuit against the chat platform Discord , seeking millions of dollars in damages over alleged failures to protect children and teenage social media users.

The $97m lawsuit, filed on Wednesday, comes after what the Brazilian government describes as failed negotiations with the company.

The complaint argues that Discord failed to abide by laws designed to protect young social media users .

“The lawsuit seeks to compel the Discord platform to adopt effective measures to protect children, adolescents, and women in the digital environment,” the government said in a statement, calling for compensation for “collective moral damages”.

The company, however, has pushed back, saying the lawsuit is excessively harsh and does not accurately depict its compliance with the country’s laws.

The lawsuit is the latest instance of a social media company facing scrutiny for allegedly exposing young users to harmful content or eroding their mental health through addictive technology products.

Critics say that tech giants have been slow to implement protective measures, despite evidence linking excessive social media use to mental health issues among young people.

In many cases, plaintiffs have argued that social media companies have prioritised user engagement and profit over health and safety concerns.

Tech companies, however, have countered that they should not be held responsible for all the content published on their platforms, nor for how users interact with the software.

In Brazil, scrutiny fell on Discord in July, after a case in the western state of Mato Grosso do Sul captured the public’s attention.

On July 22, a 13-year-old girl was on a livestream when she killed herself after being goaded to do so by a group of her fellow teenagers.

According to the Brazilian Justice Ministry, the teens first pressured her to kill an animal, but after she failed to do so, they started pushing her to take her own life.

Four teenagers and one adult have been arrested in connection with the case.

In the aftermath, Brazil’s National Data Protection Agency (ANPD) ordered Discord to suspend livestream services on August 12. First Lady Rosangela Lula da Silva also called for the site to be taken down.

The messaging platform, which hosts about 90 million active daily users, said that it would stop streaming services and take steps “to make Discord safer for teens”.

But the Brazilian government said that the company “continues to exhibit flaws in its age verification and user protection mechanisms”.

The ANPD also fined TikTok $30m on Tuesday for child privacy violations, an indicator of the more aggressive approach the Brazilian government has taken on such issues.

articles.title: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, who filled the world with polka dots, dead at 97
articles.summary: Yayoi Kusama, one of the world’s most celebrated and best-selling artists, has died age 97, according to a statement on the artist’s official website.
articles.body: Yayoi Kusama, one of the world’s most celebrated and best-selling artists, has died age 97, according to a statement on the artist’s official website. “It is with profound sorrow that (we announce) the passing of Yayoi Kusama at a hospital in Tokyo on August 14,” read the statement, posted on Thursday. Kusama was, by the time of her death, one of contemporary art’s most popular and commercially successful figures. Her famous “Infinity Mirror Rooms,” large-scale installations that immersed audiences in endlessly repeating reflections of color and light, attracted millions of gallery visitors. Her distinctive pumpkin sculptures and polka-dot paintings, meanwhile, generated millions of dollars in auction revenue. But the global recognition of her work in later years was made all the more remarkable by the difficulties she overcame to achieve it, namely childhood trauma, mental illness and years of relative obscurity. Born into a dysfunctional and abusive household in 1929, Kusama spent much of her childhood in a military factory sewing parachutes for Japan’s imperial army during World War II. She was, by this time, experiencing vivid hallucinations, which flooded her world with the polka-dots that would later characterize her work. Despite briefly studying the modernist “nihonga” painting style at art school in Kyoto, Kusama had little formal training — or apparent interest — in Japanese art traditions. From the earliest stages of her career, she instead experimented with abstraction and the repeated dot patterns seen in her celebrated “Infinity Nets” paintings. Encouraged by a letter exchange with American artist Georgia O’Keeffe, and disillusioned with life in postwar Japan, the 27-year-old moved to America in the late 1950s, arriving in Seattle before relocating to New York amid the genesis of the pop art movement. She proceeded to turn the city’s abstract impressionist tradition on its head in a storm of dots, flowers and phallic protrusions, producing a significant body of work that included not only paintings and sculptures, but surreal works of film, literature and performance art. In keeping with 1960s counterculture, Kusama staged “happenings” in which she transformed naked bodies into dotted canvases. She also famously sent an open letter to US President Richard Nixon in 1968 offering to have sex with him if he stopped the Vietnam war. “Let’s forget ourselves, dearest Richard,” she wrote, “and become one with the Absolute, all together in the alltogether (sic).” Nixon appears not to have taken up the offer. (The war did not end until 1975, with the Fall of Saigon.) But such episodes demonstrated that, although Kusama’s work was full of joy and color, she was unafraid to address key battlegrounds of the day: gender equality, gay rights and the anti-war movement. The art establishment often drew on, if not directly copied, Kusama’s work. But it never fully embraced her. Despite counting the likes of Andy Warhol and Donald Judd as friends, she remained an outsider. As the Guggenheim Museum’s senior curator of Asian art, Alexandra Munroe, wrote in a CNN profile for Kusama’s 90th birthday in 2018: “Besides being a foreign woman of color from a chastened Asian power, the psychological content of (Kusama’s) work set her identity apart from the Western mainstream that wrote the first histories of the 1960s avant-garde.” Kusama returned to Japan in the early 1970s and quickly vanished from public view. Within a few years, she had checked herself into a psychiatric hospital where she continued to live voluntarily. A compulsive, prolific artist who rarely drafted paintings before starting them, Kusama continued to produce art from the facility and a small studio nearby. And after more than a decade in the wilderness, the late 1980s heralded a major revaluation of her work. Viewed through a contemporary lens, Kusama’s art was afforded new recognition. Her long-forgotten paintings were resurrected at Western exhibitions, including a high-profile 1989 career retrospective at New York’s Center for International Contemporary Arts. In 1993, the international art world’s belated approval was seemingly cemented when she was asked to represent Japan at the Venice Biennale — an event that, 27 years earlier, she had essentially gatecrashed by unofficially exhibiting 1,500 mirrored balls on the lawn outside the Italian Pavilion (officials even intervened to block her attempts to sell the plastic globes for $2 each). The value of her output, in turn, rose dramatically. In May 2022, an early painting “Untitled (Nets)” sold for almost $10.5 million, setting an auction record for her work. She was also consistently among the world’s best-selling artists, with her work fetching a combined $190.5 million at auctions, from Hong Kong to New York, in 2023 alone. While many of her New York contemporaries faded from cultural relevance, Kusama’s only grew in her later years. Her pumpkins were sought out, often at great cost, as centerpieces for museums, cultural districts and real estate developments (among those sculptures was one that was infamously blown into the sea off Japan’s Naoshima island by a typhoon in 2021), while a museum dedicated to her work opened in Tokyo in 2017. Selfies taken in the artist’s “Infinity Mirror Rooms” meanwhile flooded Instagram. Luxury collaborations with Louis Vuitton and a major 2018 documentary “Kusama: Infinity” saw her face posted across billboards and movie theaters, respectively. Kusama may have been an artist ahead of her time, but the world finally caught up. News of her death rippled across social media, with many paying tribute. Munroe, who had organized a landmark retrospective in the US of the artist’s work in the the late 1980s, said in an Instagram post that “her stories changed how the history of avant-garde art was written and understood.” Meanwhile David Zwirner, whose galleries hosted numerous Kusama exhibitions, recalled visitors waiting in “hour-long lines for the chance to experience her work.” “At the time of her passing, Kusama was, without a doubt, the most famous living artist in the world,” he posted on Instagram.

articles.title: Yayoi Kusama: Japanese avant-garde artist dies aged 97
articles.summary: Her colourful creations drew large crowds and fetched some of the highest ever prices for a female artist.
articles.body:
Japanese avant-garde artist Yayoi Kusama, who became famous for her colourful polka dot-covered sculptures and installations, has died at the age of 97.

Kusama, who had voluntarily lived in a psychiatric hospital for decades, was known for her bright red wig and her giant, quirky creations.

Her exhibitions drew large crowds around the world, and her vibrant works fetched some of the highest ever prices for a female artist.

A statement from her company said: "Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant-garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry."

Kusama died at a hospital in Tokyo on 14 August, the statement said.

It added: "She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul.

"We will carry forward Kusama's wishes and, through art, continue to bring hope and strength for the future to people around the world."

In pictures: The dotty world of Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama

Kusama became one of the world's most recognisable artists and a global cultural icon in her 80s and 90s, after having been mostly overlooked for decades.

Poorly received by a masculine-dominated art scene of New York in the 1960s, Kusama caused a stir with her exhibitions of phallic sculptures, including a fabric couch, and frequent displays of nudity.

In 1965, her work "Infinity Mirror Rooms", in which mirrors and lights create seemingly endless spaces, attracted millions of visitors. Later, her polka dot and pumpkin works became highly sought-after.

However, she became distressed when her ideas were copied by or "inspired" her male contemporaries – including Andy Warhol, Claes Oldenburg and Lucas Samaras – whose works would be displayed at more prestigious galleries.

After spending years watching male artists gain recognition for her work, she returned home to Japan – feeling dejected and distraught.

She entered a psychiatric facility receiving treatment for mental illnesses, where she would live and work for the remainder of her life.

Miraculously, she managed to find a hospital where the doctors were interested in art therapy and checked herself in. Such a secure environment allowed her to focus on creating art.

Through the 1970s and early 80s, her work depicted uncharacteristically dark series' of collages in which she embraced the imagery of natural life cycles.

Kusama went on to become Japan's first solo artist to represent the country at the 1993 Venice Biennale. Twenty-seven years earlier, she had turned up, uninvited, and laid down 1,500 mirror balls on the ground.

The roaring success of the exhibition led to a huge transformation in how she was received both in Japan and abroad.

In 2001, she was awarded the Asahi Prize – recognising outstanding cultural, academic and artistic contributions in Japan.

One of her paintings fetched about $10.5m (£7.7m) at auction in 2022, making her works some of the highest-earning in the world for a female artist.

She held major exhibitions around the world, including at the Tate Modern gallery in London, which was ran for three years after being extended several times because of its popularity.

Catherine Wood, interim director of Tate Modern, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday it was "our most visited exhibition of all time because people really love Kusama's work".

The exhibition invited visitors into the artist's Infinity Mirror Rooms.

"You would step in there and the lights would go down, and it felt like you were looking into the mysteries of the Universe," Wood said. "She was very good at conjuring this sense of wonder and infinity that she was obsessed with."

As a child, Kusama experienced hallucinations of embers and flashing – later using her art as a vehicle for others to understand her vision of the world.

"One day, after seeing a tablecloth with a red flower pattern on a desk, I saw the same red flower pattern all over the ceiling, windows and pillars. It filled the room, and covered my body," she wrote in her autobiography.

Kusama was born in 1929 in the rural provincial town of Matsumoto, based in the central Nagano region of Japan.

Her parents did not support her early moves to study painting in Kyoto.

She was later told her artistry caused great shame to her conservative family. Some elements of the US press also criticised what they perceived as an endless desire for publicity – either in her messaging promoting peace or critiquing the art establishment.

The world, along with her native Japan, radically changed its perception of Kusama in her later life.

Social media fuelled a spike in interest over recent years – with her museum's bold floral shapes and shiny steel orbs turning into a desired backdrop for selfies and poses.

Among her many motifs, the pumpkin has become iconic in her works. To her, the vegetable represented comfort and nostalgia.

She once said in an interview: "Pumpkins speak to me.

"They embody a sense of stability and gives me peace of mind."

articles.title: Before and after: Satellite images show how Nepal’s green mountainside turned into debris field
articles.summary: South Asia News: Satellite images taken before and after the deadly flash flood near Nepal’s border with Tibet reveal a striking change in the landscape: stretches of .
articles.body: Satellite images taken before and after the deadly flash flood near Nepal’s border with Tibet reveal a striking change in the landscape: stretches of green mountainside visible before the disaster are now covered by a broad expanse of brown debris and sediment.The Planet Labs imagery has provided early clues to how the disaster may have started. Experts examining the pictures believe that the lower section of a glacier broke away high in the mountains and plunged hundreds of metres into the valley below, likely carrying or entraining rock and sediment as it fell.Early reports raised an earthquake as a possible trigger, but the US Geological Survey later said the recorded seismic activity came from the collapse itself rather than a separate earthquake, according to news agency Reuters.Satellite pictures point to the starting pointSikkim University academic Vikram Gupta, an engineering geology specialist, said the satellite evidence indicated that the collapse began at the glacier’s lower end."It’s confirmed that a substantial portion of that glacier snout collapsed to initiate the event - probably including or entraining a fair amount of rock and sediment," Gupta said.Dan Shugar, an earth scientist and associate professor at the University of Calgary, also traced the apparent origin of the disaster to a glacier high above the valley."What I can see in this morning's satellite imagery from Planet Labs, the lower part of a glacier broke off at about 5,200 metres and crashed onto the valley floor about 1,200 metres below," Shugar said.The resulting ice-rock avalanche sent a destructive surge downstream, eventually carrying water, sediment and boulders through the river systems below.A Planet Labs pair taken a day apart captures the border valleys on August 25 and August 26, effectively bracketing the disaster. Other comparisons track the transformation of Manakamana and Khadga Bhanjyang between August 23 and August 26.Floodwaters surged through communities along the Bhote Koshi. Rasuwa and nearby districts suffered widespread damage, including to transport links, homes and power infrastructure.Snow cover changed sharply before disasterThe satellite imagery also showed another significant change in the mountains in the hours before the flood.Comparing satellite images taken roughly a day apart, Shugar noticed a pronounced loss of snow cover."Some of the glaciers in the valley were covered in snow yesterday and today they are mostly bare ice. So in other words (and I haven't seen any weather station data yet), it was probably warm," he said.Whether those warmer conditions contributed directly to the collapse has not yet been established.Nepal’s glaciers have already been undergoing significant long-term changes. A 2023 United Nations assessment found that Nepal’s snow-covered mountains had lost nearly a third of their ice over a little more than three decades because of global warming.It also found that Nepal's glaciers melted 65% faster over the preceding decade than during the decade before it.Seismic signal traced to the collapseAn initial assessment by Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority indicated that an ice-and-rock landslide triggered the debris-laden flood in the Lhende River, around 20 kilometres northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing.Prakash Pokharel, a geologist with the authority who reviewed the Planet Labs images, identified the immediate event as an avalanche involving both ice and rock."The flash floods were caused by an ice-rock avalanche on the Nepali side," Pokharel said.The USGS assessment provided further clarity on the early earthquake theory. What had initially been identified as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake was subsequently determined to be seismic activity produced by the collapse of glacial rock and ice and the movement of debris, rather than a separate quake preceding the disaster.Shugar said construction activity could also be a factor. On the broader question of global warming, he said "whether climate change played a role is something we will no doubt be looking into in the near future".Search for hundreds still missingSearch teams have struggled to reach parts of the disaster zone, where poor weather and communications failures have complicated efforts to locate survivors and assess the damage. Rescue helicopters were also unable to land in Syapru Besi and Timure as conditions and disrupted access hampered operations.Rasuwa, a mountainous district of roughly 50,000 people, is also home to several hydropower projects in areas hit hardest by the disaster.By late Wednesday, police in Nepal had recovered 157 bodies. More than 400 tourists were still unaccounted for in Nepal, with tourism officials saying around 340 were foreigners.Many of those caught in the disaster were travelling through the region on pilgrimages to Kailash Mansarovar.Across the border in Tibet, Chinese state media reported three deaths and 265 people missing in Gyirong, while cautioning that the toll was still being verified. The mudslide also severed road, communications and power connections in the border area.Surge sent water levels soaringAccording to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, floodwaters swept sediment and boulders into both the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems as the surge travelled downstream.At Galchhi, the river reportedly climbed roughly nine metres — about 30 feet — in half an hour.India evacuates thousands, offers Nepal assistanceDownstream concerns also reached India. Disaster-response units were put on alert in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh as officials watched for the flood surge from Nepal to enter the Gandak river system.An earlier Central Water Commission advisory, issued after a sudden rise in the Trishuli at Furke Khola, about 160 kilometres from India, had raised the possibility of glacial lake outburst flood activity near the Nepal-China border.Districts along the Gandak's downstream course in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh were told to maintain heightened surveillance.About 5,000 residents had already been moved to safety from six Bihar districts by Thursday, with preparations covering as many as 10,000 to 12,000 people if further evacuations were required.Prime Minister Narendra Modi conveyed condolences to Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah and offered humanitarian assistance, saying Indian teams were working with Nepalese authorities on rescue and relief.The disaster also comes against a backdrop of more frequent and increasingly powerful extreme events across the Hindu Kush Himalayas, including floods, landslides, avalanches and droughts.For now, the satellite record is helping investigators reconstruct how the catastrophe unfolded — from the apparent collapse of ice and rock high in the mountains to the destructive torrent that swept through valleys, settlements and river systems far downstream.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
